A.T. Resource Grid

What we know about the Appalachian Trail corridor, one square mile at a time.

    About this data

    Every dataset here is summarized on the same grid, so a single cell can be read across vegetation, citizen-science records, unique species and land administrators. The grid is NatureServe's nested hexagon system: a one square mile hexagon, a cluster of seven hexagons (7 sq mi), and a cluster of seven clusters (49 sq mi). Cell IDs are the NatureServe IDs, so the numbers here join back to the source tables.

    What each layer is

    LayerSourceKeep in mind
    Land administratorsA.T. corridor lands and tractsLists who administers at least one mapped acre in a cell, with each one's share of the cell's mapped land. Generalized to the grid; not a boundary record.
    VegetationNPS vegetation map for the A.T., by mapped vegetation typeThe map stops at the edge of the surveyed lands, so most cells are only partly covered.
    iNaturalistResearch-grade records, Records follow people. Few records means few visits, not few species.
    eBirdChecklists, Same caution. Thinly sampled cells are faded on the bird maps.
    Unique speciesRare species priority zonesRates how fragile the populations of unique species are in each cell, from plant and animal records. Shown at 7 and 49 sq mi only. A screening aid, not a survey result.

    Reading the maps

    • Cell colors fade as you zoom in, so the basemap shows through. At the closest zoom the fill is 75% transparent and the white cell outlines remain.
    • Filled cells have data for the measure on screen. Outlined cells have data in another layer but none for this measure.
    • Colors are five equal-count classes of the cells with data at the cell size on screen, so the classes change when you change cell size.
    • The strip under the map runs from Springer Mountain to Katahdin. Each bar is a ten-mile stretch, averaged from the 49 sq mi cells.
    • The search box finds birds, invasive plants, forest pests and vegetation types in every cell where they were recorded. Other iNaturalist species are only searchable where they rank among a cell's ten most-recorded, so those results are partial. Rare species are not searchable.
    • Species names link to Wikipedia, looked up by scientific name. A name with no article of its own opens a Wikipedia search instead.
    • Trail miles are measured along the mapped centerline and are approximate.

    Updates

    iNaturalist and eBird summaries are refreshed quarterly. This page shows the run.
